question: The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report No 17/2026 on rescEU1 – the EU’s civil protection reserve of strategic assets and stockpiles for when national capacities fall short – highlights several weaknesses in the planning, governance and assessment of EU-funded capacities. In light of this: 1.

How does the Commission justify funding new rescEU capacities without a harmonised methodology that enables the prior assessment of existing national capacities and prevents duplication with national civil protection schemes?

What performance indicators does it intend to put in place in order to objectively assess the cost, mobilisation time and operational added value of rescEU stockpiles, in comparison with the direct mobilisation of assets held by Member States?

Does it intend to make any future development of rescEU conditional on a prior demonstration of its economic and operational effectiveness, in accordance with the recommendations of the European Court of Auditors, in order to ensure the proper use of EU funds and compliance with the principle of subsidiarity?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) The Commission, together with the Member States and participating states of the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), undertakes a comprehensive capacity gap analysis, also in relation to existing national capacities1.

A common methodology, adapted to the specificities of the different sectors, is applied for such a gap analysis, by gathering data shared by Member States and participating states, as they consider it possible based on the sensitivity of the information. In addition, the Commission continuously analyses the response to the requests for assistance under the UCPM to further assess possible gaps.

If new rescEU2 capacities are deemed essential to address these gaps, in agreement with Member States and participating states, the Commission establishes a strategy – in line with the EU Stockpiling Strategy3 – and allocates funds for their development.

rescEU's performance is assessed through key indicators, which include timely mobilisation, as well as identification of capacity gaps and critical needs where Member States' capacities are unavailable or insufficient. Mobilisation timelines4 are tailored to the assistance’s nature, with associated costs covered by the Commission5.

The economic and operational effectiveness of the existing capacities is a key condition for the future development of rescEU. To ensure that the standards of performance are preserved and further strengthened, the Commission fully acknowledges the added value of the European Court of Auditors’ recommendations.
These insights will be given due consideration for future actions, jointly with Member States and participating states.
1 Including those pre-committed to the European Civil Protection Pool in line with the Regulation (EU)
